This is the full-sample estimation; the authors state that their inferences on the specialization comparison are mainly based on the specialist/non-specialist subsample analyses. The all-sample column establishes the overall tenure association before the specialist/non-specialist comparison.

evidence.quote: Since absolute values of discretionary accruals used as a dependent variable are truncated at zero, a truncated regression approach is adopted to arrive at unbiased estimates of coefficients in the model.
Consequently our inferences are mainly drawn based on the sub-sample analyses.

preprocessing.description: All continuous variables are winsorized at three standard deviations.

evidence.quote: All continuous variables are winsorized at three standard deviations.

scope.quote: In this study, we examine whether industry specialization of auditors and low balling affect the association between auditor tenure and earnings quality.
main tests are based on the discretionary accruals model suggested by Ball and Shivakumar (2006).
We expect the coefficient for Tenure to be negative, suggesting shorter tenure is associated with higher discretionary accruals, i.e. lower earnings quality.
Additionally, we expect this association to be significantly weaker for firms audited by industry specialists.
We conduct tests based on both specialist and non-specialist sub-samples, as well as on the full sample with an interaction term between tenure and specialists.
Consequently our inferences are mainly drawn based on the sub-sample analyses.

method.quote: Estimations are based on truncated regression approach.

equation.quote: ABSTDA 1⁄4 a þ b1Tenure þ b2Age þ b3Size þ b4Size2 þ b5Size3 þ b6IndGrow þ b7Grow
þ b8CFO þ bjIndustryDum þ bkYearDum þ � (2)

sample.quote: This study is based on a sample of firms from 1993 to 2004.
We include only firms that are audited by Big 6/5/4 auditors
Firms with mergers and acquisitions (M&A) are dropped from the sample
Our final sample consists of 32,777 firm-year observations.
Out of the total sample, 24,433 firm-year observations are audited by non-specialists and 8344 firm-year observations by industry specialists.
A Big N audit firm’s industry specialization is measured based on its share of clients’ total assets in the two-digit SIC industry group

scope.quote: In this study, we examine whether industry specialization of auditors and low balling affect the association between auditor tenure and earnings quality.
main tests are based on the discretionary accruals model suggested by Ball and Shivakumar (2006).
We expect the coefficient for Tenure to be negative, suggesting shorter tenure is associated with higher discretionary accruals, i.e. lower earnings quality.
Additionally, we expect this association to be significantly weaker for firms audited by industry specialists.
We conduct tests based on both specialist and non-specialist sub-samples, as well as on the full sample with an interaction term between tenure and specialists.
Consequently our inferences are mainly drawn based on the sub-sample analyses.

review_notes: Selected the Table 2 family: the All column estimates the overall tenure–ABSTDA association, and the Non-specialists/Specialists columns are the source-supported core comparison for whether specialization weakens it. Section 4.3 states that the authors' inferences are mainly drawn from those two subgroup fits; footnote 20 explains the pooled-interaction precision concern. Table 3's full-sample model interacts Specialist with tenure and controls as a complementary test, not the authors' main inferential design. The low-balling section is a separately introduced test and later models are sensitivity/endogeneity analyses.

The Ball–Shivakumar Equation (1) fit is retained as a supporting construction model because its residual generates discretionary accruals used to form ABSTDA. Equation (1)'s full RHS, including the alpha-10 product, and the IndGrow industry-sales ratio are now supported by the independent coordinator-verified reading amendment 003.
